result:
Alright, then I'll write about useless beautiful things.

I have a deep affection for things that do absolutely nothing. A chipped blue mug that leaks just enough that you can't actually drink from it. A ticket stub from a train you took years ago to a city you barely remember. A smooth stone from a beach whose name you've forgotten. They don't earn their keep. They just sit there, on a shelf or at the bottom of a drawer, quietly refusing to be practical.

I think we keep them because they are proof that not everything in our lives has to be optimized.

The world is very good right now at asking: *What is this for? How does it scale? Is it efficient?* And those are fine questions for bridges and spreadsheets. But they're terrible questions for a life.

A life needs some loose threads.

It needs the afternoon you spent doing nothing productive except watching rain make patterns on a window. It needs the song you love not because it's good, exactly, but because you were nineteen and driving at night and it came on and suddenly the whole summer felt enormous. It needs the recipe you copied out by hand even though you could have taken a photo, because your handwriting that day was loopy and happy and you don't write like that anymore.

I like secondhand bookstores for this reason. Not the curated, pretty ones — the real ones, where books are stacked in teetering piles and someone has left a pressed leaf between pages 112 and 113, and a note in the margin that just says "no!!" next to a paragraph you thought was perfectly reasonable. Someone else lived in that book before you. They argued with it. They got bored or moved house or died, and the book kept going anyway.

That's what useless beautiful things do. They keep going.

They remind us that we were paying attention, once. That on an ordinary Tuesday, something caught our eye — a color, a sound, a shell shaped exactly like a tiny ear — and we thought, *oh, that's worth holding onto,* even if we couldn't explain why.

Maybe especially because we couldn't explain why.

If I ever have a house with a porch, I want it to be cluttered with these things. Wind chimes that are slightly out of tune. A plant I'm keeping alive out of sheer stubbornness. Chairs that don't match. A drawer — every house needs one — full of string and batteries that may or may not work and keys that open nothing anyone can remember.

Not hoarding. Just honoring.

Honoring the idea that a person is not a product. That memory isn't storage. That beauty doesn't need a business plan.

So keep the stone. Keep the leaking mug. Write the thing in your notebook that you know no one will ever read, in your worst handwriting, just because the thought felt true for about ten seconds on a train.

Those ten seconds count.
